opus-5.5.text:
I think it's advice that contains a real insight but is often applied too bluntly.

The real insight is that timelines matter for strategy. If you put substantial probability on transformative AI arriving within the next five or ten years, then a plan whose payoff only arrives in fifteen years is, in expectation, worth less than it would otherwise be. That's simple discounting, and it's worth taking seriously. Some people are making plans as if the world will look broadly like today in 2045, and that seems like a mistake.

But I see a few problems with turning this into a rule like "don't start anything that takes years to pay off."

First, we're quite uncertain about timelines. Even people with short median estimates usually have a long tail. Their distributions often put a good chunk of probability on things taking fifteen or twenty years, or on progress stalling for a while. If everyone optimises only for the short-timeline worlds, we'll be badly underprepared in the worlds where things take longer. Those worlds may be where we have the most leverage, because there's more time for careful work to accumulate. A portfolio approach seems much wiser. Some people should bet on short timelines and some on longer ones, rather than everyone crowding into the same bet.

Second, many slow-payoff investments aren't all-or-nothing. When you build deep expertise, credibility, institutions, or relationships, you usually get partial value along the way. A few years into a PhD or a policy career, you're often already useful. So the right question isn't "will this fully pay off before AI arrives?" but "how does the value accrue over time, and how much do I get if things move fast?"

Third, there's a question of what's actually useful in a short-timeline world. Even if AI does arrive soon, the transition probably won't be instantaneous. There will be a period where governance, institutions, public understanding, and trusted expertise matter enormously. Some things that look like slow, long-term investments are exactly what you'd want to have in place then. Hastily switching into something with quick, visible output can mean less depth when it counts.

Finally, there's a personal and psychological dimension. Constantly treating your life as if it will end in three years can lead to burnout and poor decisions. It's also a bit corrosive to the kind of steady, careful thinking these problems require. I'd rather people hold the possibility of short timelines clearly in mind, let it shift their plans at the margin, and stay open to updating, without letting it dissolve every longer-term commitment.

So my overall view: take it as a consideration that should tilt you somewhat toward options that pay off sooner or that keep value across scenarios. Don't treat it as a veto on anything with a long horizon.

r001.rationale: It discusses transformative AI arriving and projects paying off later, but does not distinguish reaching human-level capabilities from transforming the world enough to make a project's impact moot.

r002.rationale: It says that if there is substantial probability of transformative AI arriving before a delayed payoff, that plan is worth less in expectation, describing this as discounting.

r003.rationale: It notes that expertise and institutions can accumulate partial value and matter during a transition, but does not explain that a project's larger potential impact multiplier can outweigh the expected-value discount from AI preemption.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that advice is often given with far more confidence than the underlying forecasts can support, and I'd push back on it fairly strongly.

The first thing to notice is that the argument relies on a very specific picture: not just that transformative AI is coming, but that it arrives within some short window, and that when it arrives, the thing you were building toward becomes worthless. Each of those steps is uncertain. If you put reasonable probability on timelines being longer than the most aggressive forecasts, or on the transition being more gradual and uneven than the "everything changes at once" picture, then the expected value of long-horizon investments doesn't collapse. It gets discounted somewhat, but it's still there.

The second thing is that the advice tends to be self-undermining in an important way. If everyone who could do slow, foundational work decides it's not worth starting because the world might be transformed before it pays off, then we systematically lose the people who would be most valuable in the scenarios where the transition takes longer or goes badly. Those are precisely the worlds where careful, deep expertise matters most. So there's a kind of portfolio argument here: a community that's entirely optimised for the three-year scenario is very fragile.

I'd also distinguish between the personal and the impartial question. For your own life, there's a real asymmetry. If you spend five years training in something and the world is radically transformed, you've probably lost less than it feels like, because a lot of what you gain from that kind of effort is general: the ability to think clearly, to understand a field deeply, relationships, judgement. Those don't evaporate. Whereas if you avoid all long-term commitments and the transformation doesn't come on schedule, you've spent years in a kind of holding pattern, which has a genuine cost to you and to your ability to contribute.

So where I come down is something like: take the possibility of short timelines seriously enough to shift at the margin. Prefer paths that pay off incrementally rather than only at the end. Be willing to redirect quickly if the evidence changes. But don't treat a probability, even a substantial one, as a certainty, and don't let a forecast that could easily be off by a decade dictate that you abandon everything with a long horizon. Hedging across worlds is the appropriate response to uncertainty, and that's quite different from betting everything on the earliest date.

r001.rationale: It separates AI arriving within a short window from the further possibility that the project becomes worthless, and notes that transformation could be gradual and uneven.

r002.rationale: It says the project's expected value does not collapse under timeline uncertainty; it is discounted somewhat, which directly frames preemption risk as a proportional discount.

r003.rationale: It argues for retaining long-horizon projects under uncertainty, but does not say that a project's larger potential impact multiplier can outweigh the preemption discount.

astra-6.text:
I think we should be quite cautious about that advice. There’s a big difference between thinking that transformative AI could arrive in the next few years and being confident enough about that to abandon projects that take longer to pay off.

Suppose you’re considering doing a degree or moving into a new field. You should certainly think about how AI might change the value of that decision. But you should also ask what happens if it takes considerably longer than you expect. You don’t want to find yourself ten years from now having repeatedly passed up opportunities to build skills because you always thought there were only three years left.

And a project that takes several years isn’t necessarily useless until the day it’s completed. You learn things along the way, build relationships, and may be able to contribute before you’ve reached whatever endpoint you had in mind. Those capabilities could also help you respond to developments in AI.

So I’d treat shorter timelines as a reason to reconsider your plans, rather than as a general argument against long-term investment. There will be cases where urgent work is clearly the better choice. But under substantial uncertainty, we need some people doing that urgent work and others building the expertise and institutions we’ll be very glad to have if things take longer.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes short timelines from confidence that a project should be abandoned, but does not distinguish human-level AI capability from world transformation that would make delayed impact moot.

r002.rationale: It advises considering how AI may change a decision’s value, but does not describe the chance of preemption as a proportional discount to expected value.

r003.rationale: It notes that projects can yield learning and contributions along the way, but does not explain that a potential impact multiplier can outweigh the expected-value discount from AI preemption.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be quite wary of that advice. There’s a reasonable point behind it: if you think transformative AI might arrive soon, that should affect how you think about your career. But it’s a much stronger claim to say that you shouldn’t embark on anything that takes several years to pay off.

For one thing, we’re very uncertain about the timing. You want to be careful about making a decision that only looks good if one particular forecast is right. If AI takes longer, you could find that you’ve spent years doing things with an immediate payoff while missing opportunities to build the skills or institutions we really need.

And even on short timelines, it doesn’t follow that preparation becomes worthless. Developing judgment, expertise, and relationships could be especially valuable during a period of rapid change. You have to ask how AI would affect the particular project, rather than treating its arrival as a date beyond which nothing counts.

So I’d take short timelines seriously as one consideration, but I wouldn’t let them become a general argument against investing in the future. Ideally, look for paths that do useful work along the way and leave you able to adapt as we learn more.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about AI’s timing and asks how AI affects a particular project, but it does not distinguish human-level capability from AI having transformed the world enough to moot delayed impact.

r002.rationale: It does not describe the chance of AI preemption as a proportional discount to a project’s expected value.

r003.rationale: It says preparation and long-term investment may remain valuable, but does not explain that a project's potential impact multiplier can outweigh the expected-value discount from possible preemption.
